1  THIS CRIMINAL REVISION PETITION HAVING COME UP FOR FINAL HEARING ON 12.11.2024, THE COURT ON 05.12.2024 DELIVERED THE FOLLOWING:
 2024:KER:92070  3 Crl.R.P.No.871 of 2014  P.G. AJITHKUMAR, J.

 Dated this the 5th day of December, 2024  ORDER
The accused in S.C.No.641 of 2003 on the files of the Sessions Court, Payyannur is the revision petitioner.
The Assistant Sessions Judge, Payyannur tried the petitioner on a charge for the offences punishable under Sections 306 and 498A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC).
He was convicted for the offence under Section 498A of the IPC alone.
His appeal was dismissed by the Additional Sessions Judge-I, Thalassery.
Aggrieved thereby, he has filed this revision petition under Section 397 read with Section 401 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (Code).

2. The prosecution was initiated with the following allegations:
Wife of the petitioner Smt.Sreelatha committed suicide at about 2.15 p.m. on 06.04.1999.
Their marriage was solemnised on 18.12.1995.

The petitioner subjected Smt.Sreelatha to cruelty;
2024:KER:92070 both mental and physical.
Demanding more money and gold, she was tortured.
The petitioner denied her motherhood and he had illicit relationship with his sister-in-law.
The cruelty so meted out by the petitioner had driven Smt.Sreelatha to commit suicide.
3. At the trial, PWs.1 to 14 were examined and Exts.P1 to P18 were marked on the side of the prosecution.
MOs.1 and 2 were identified also.
Exts.D1 and D2 were the documents proved on the side of the petitioner.
The petitioner contended that he was innocent and without any basis the prosecution was initiated.
The trial court considered the evidence in detail and took the view that evidence was insufficient to prove that the petitioner abetted Smt.Sreelatha to commit suicide.
It was, however, found that evidence of PWs.6 to 9 together with Exts.P6 and P9 to P12 proved that the petitioner subjected Smt.Sreelatha to cruelty, which drove her to commit suicide.

Consequently,
the petitioner was convicted for the offence under Section 498A of the IPC.
The appellate court after considering the evidence concurred with the view taken by the trial court.

sentences.text: 4. Heard the Senior Counsel appeared on instructions for the petitioner and the learned Public Prosecutor.

5. The learned Senior Counsel at the outset submitted that since the petitioner was found not guilty for the offence under Section 306 of the IPC, his conviction for the offence under Section 498A of the IPC based on the same set of facts and evidence is incorrect.

In order to fortify that contention,
the learned Senior Counsel placed reliance on Kantilal Martaji Pandor v. State of Gujarat and another [(2013) 8 SCC 781].

entities.text: Kantilal Martaji Pandor v. State of Gujarat and another [(2013) 8 SCC 781]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: That was a case where the prosecution mainly relied on a letter written by the deceased to the police station to convict the accused.
The statement of the deceased in the said letter was that the deceased was put to starvation since his income was grabbed by the accused and on account of that the deceased could not go forward.

The Apex Court held that the statements in the letter, which drove her to commit suicide was not concerning the cause of her death or as to any of the circumstances of the transaction, which resulted in her death and therefore the same was not relevant under Section 2024:KER:92070 32(1) of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.

It was further held that evidence, which essentially rests on such a dying declaration was insufficient to hold the accused guilty of the offence under Section 306 of the IPC, and for that reason no offence under Section 498A of the IPC could not also be attracted.
The evidence let in by the prosecution, for the above reason, was found insufficient to constitute cruelty as defined in Section 498A of the IPC as well.
6. In this case, the prosecution relies mainly on Ext.P6, which is a letter written by the deceased to the Sub Court, Thalassery, where the petitioner filed a petition for divorce.
A notice to appear in that case was received by the deceased.
On the eve of the date for appearance, she committed suicide.
The prosecution also relies on the evidence of PWs.7 to 9 to prove the cruelty meted out by the petitioner.
In Ext.P6 the deceased categorically maintained that the petitioner, her sister-in-law and mother-in-law were responsible for her death.
The reasons thereof have also been stated in that letter.

Matrimonial cruelties such as ill-treatment 2024:KER:92070 to coerce her to pay more money and give more gold, the petitioner's maintaining an illicit relationship with his sister-in- law (brother's wife), denial to her matrimony and motherhood, etc. are stated in Ext.P6.

After narrating various incidents concerning the aforementioned acts of harassment and ill-treatment, it has been stated that she did not want to be a burden to the petitioner and therefore she decided to commit suicide.
7. As rightly pointed out by the learned senior counsel for the petitioner in our tradition bound society having affinity to one's elder sister in law need not always be suspicious.
However, when such an affinity grows to the extent of ignorance and neglect towards his wife to the height of her intolerance that amounts to cruelty.
When that eventuated to the suicide of his wife that becomes a punishable offence.

In the said circumstances, the statements in Ext.P6, if they were made by the deceased and true, certainly would amount to cruelty coming within the purview of clause (a) of Explanation to Section 498A of the IPC.
Of course, the question whether 2024:KER:92070 the said letter is relevant under Section 32(1) of the Evidence Act also is germane for consideration.

8. As observed in Kantilal Martaji Pandor [(2013) 8 SCC 781] a statement made by a person, who is no more, as to the cause of her death, or as to any of the circumstances of the transaction resulting Rameshan vs State Of Kerala on 5 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/136456746/
3 in her death alone is relevant under Section 32(1) of the Evidence Act.
Of course, the relevancy of such a statement arises only in cases in which the cause of death of that person comes into question.

In the said decision, the letter written by the deceased was not accepted as a statement under Section 32(1) of the Evidence Act holding that the statement therein was not about the cause of death of the deceased.
Whereas, here the specific assertions in Ext.P6 are concerning the circumstances leading to her committing suicide.
The fact that she committed suicide by consuming poison is undisputed or rather stands proved.

Several instances amounting to mental and physical harassment of the deceased suffered at the hands of the petitioner have been narrated in Ext.P6,
which is 2024:KER:92070 proved to be in her handwriting.
When it is categorically stated in Ext.P6
that such circumstances led to her committing suicide and the letter was written by her on the eve of her suicide
, there cannot be a different view than that it is relevant under Section 32(1) of the Evidence Act.
9. PW7 is the brother and PW8 is the elder sister of the deceased.
PW9 is the husband of her another sister.
These witnesses deposed having intervened in the matrimonial dispute between the petitioner and Smt.Sreelatha.

They claimed that Smt.Sreelatha told them about the ill-treatment,
including assault perpetrated on her by the petitioner.
Of course, none of them was a witness to any of such incidents.
But they had intervened in the dispute.
Particularly, PW9 was approached by the petitioner's brother and another for conciliation.

Thus, the claim of PWs.7 to 9 is that they knew about the cruelty meted out by the petitioner from the deceased and the attending circumstances,
and the same circumstances eventually resulted in her death.
In such circumstances, the statements of those witnesses before the 2024:KER:92070 court concerning such acts of cruelty becomes relevant and cannot be ignored as mere hearsay information.
10. Along with the aforementioned evidence, Exts.P9 to P12, which are also proved to be the writings of the deceased, were placed on reliance by the prosecution.
Of course, the statements therein are mostly indicative of a cordial relationship between the petitioner and the deceased.
A marital relationship where the spouses lived together for quite some time, it cannot be expected that the parties would have behaved with hostility all throughout.
When in Ext.P6 letter, which was written by the deceased immediately prior to her committing suicide, she spelled out the instances of ill- treatment and harassment, the same reflects the real facts.
Therefore, the statements in Exts.P9 to P12 cannot be given more emphasis than that are contained in Ext.P6.
As stated, the incidents narrated in Ext.P6 certainly amount to cruelty attracting the penal provision under Section 498A of the IPC.
The courts below after analysing the said evidence found that the petitioner has committed the offence.
The findings are 2024:KER:92070 well reasoned.
I find no reason to interfere with the said concurrent finding in the exercise of the powers of revision.
The conviction is therefore confirmed.
11. The petitioner was sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of three years and to pay a fine of Rs.10,000/-.

Having regard to the delay occasioned after the incident, the age of the petitioner and other mitigating circumstances, I am of the view that the period of imprisonment can be reduced by modifying the sentence.
Accordingly, this revision petition is allowed in part.
The conviction of the petitioner under Section 498A of the IPC is confirmed.
He is sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of one year and to pay a fine of Rs.10,000/-.
In default of Rameshan vs State Of Kerala on 5 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/136456746/
4 payment of fine
, he shall undergo rigorous imprisonment for a further period of three months.
